descriptions are presented in Appendix A. Cash taxes vary with profitability, with more profitable firms expected to pay higher
taxes. We scale cash taxes by pretax book income to reflect this relation, which is particularly important in our setting because
financial constraints are often associated with declines in firm profitability. Scaling cash taxes by pretax book income directly
controls for reduced taxes due to declining profitability during financially constrained periods. Prior to computing the change,
CashETRs above 1 (below �1) are reset to 1 (�1). <sup>11</sup> As discussed by Hanlon and Heitzman (2010) in their review of the tax
literature, it is important to select a tax planning measure appropriate to the research question and not simply apply a laundry
list of measures. We utilize cash ETRs because we are interested in how firms respond to financial constraints that result in a
need to generate additional cash. A firm’s cash ETR is the most direct measure of a firm’s cash tax burden. Tax planning that
decreases a firm’s cash tax burden will have a direct impact on a firm’s cash ETR.

Financial Constraints

The variable of interest in Equation (1), DConstraint, captures the change in financial constraints faced by the firm. We
measure DConstraint using two firm-specific measures, RankDZ and RankDKZ, and one macroeconomic measure, Tightening.
We measure the change in financial constraints in year t�1 (i.e., the change from year t�2 to year t�1) because firms generally
need time to plan and implement tax planning strategies. <sup>12</sup> The measures are constructed so that higher values represent an
increase in financial constraints. RankDKZ is intended to capture changes in firms’ investment-related constraints and equals the
decile rank of the change in the firm’s investment-related constraints, based on the Kaplan and Zingales (1997) financial
constraint index. Decile rank values range from 0 to 9. RankDZ is intended to capture changes in firms’ financial constraints
arising from financial distress and equals the decile rank of the change in the firm’s Altman (1968) distress prediction Z-score.
We use decile ranks of the firm-specific measures because the distribution of both the underlying constraint measures and the
changes in the measures are highly skewed (see means and medians in Table 2, Panels A and B). Tightening is based on data
from the Federal Reserve Board’s Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey and is intended to capture changes in a firm’s financial
constraints due to changing macroeconomic conditions that impact the cost and accessibility of external debt financing.
Tightening equals the average net percentage of domestic respondents reporting tightening standards during the year for
commercial and industrial loans. <sup>13</sup> Although the firm-specific measures directly capture changes in firm-specific constraints, the
macroeconomic measure provides insight into the revenue effects of tax planning due to changing macroeconomic conditions
and improves identification, as macroeconomic constraints are exogenous to the firm.

Regardless of whether the increased constraints are due to firm-specific investment needs, firm-specific distress, or
changing macroeconomic conditions, our arguments predict a negative association between changes in financial constraints and
changes in cash ETRs.


Controls

Controls


In addition to our explanatory variable of interest, DConstraint, we include a battery of control variables in our regression
model. All changes in control variables are measured contemporaneously with the change in cash ETRs (i.e., from year t�1 to
year t). We include three variables—DPROA, DSalesGrowth, and DLnSales—to control for the change in the underlying
economic activity of the firm to ensure that any documented association between tax planning and financial constraints is due to
the presence of the constraint and not a decrease in economic activity. Recall, also, that our dependent variable, DCashETR,
equals the change in the ratio of cash taxes paid to pretax income. By scaling by pretax income when computing a firm’s cash
ETR, we directly control for reduced taxes due to reduced profitability.

DPROA equals the change in a firm’s pretax return on assets and controls for the effect of firm profitability on cash taxes.

positive coefficient on DPROA. We also include DSalesGrowth, which equals the change in a firm’s sales growth for the
period, as an additional control for any effect of a change in economic activity on cash ETRs.

DLnSales equals the changes in a firm’s natural log of sales and controls for changes in firm size. Prior studies generally
argue that firm size can have two opposing effects on tax planning. On one hand, large firms are often more sophisticated and
better equipped to structure complex tax-reduction transactions (Mills, Erickson, and Maydew 1998; Hanlon, Mills, and
Slemrod 2007), suggesting a positive association between firm size and tax planning. On the other hand, large firms are often
more mature and have fewer tax shields as their capital investment slows, suggesting a negative relation between firm size and
tax planning. Prior studies often use the natural log of sales, assets, or the market value of equity to proxy for firm size. We
selected the natural log of sales in this study because, unlike assets and the market value of equity, sales represent a current-year
flow that captures the overall economic activity of the firm. Because DLnSales captures many effects, we make no directional
prediction.

We also include the change in a firm’s book-to-market ratio, DBM, to capture the change in a firm’s expected future
economic growth. While growth firms face different tax planning incentives and opportunities than mature firms, we make no
directional prediction for DBM.

We also include a variety of variables that are standard controls in tax planning models. DForeign proxies for the change in
the extent of a firm’s foreign operations. DForeign equals the change in a firm’s ratio of foreign pretax income to assets.
Because multinational firms can locate income in lower tax jurisdictions, we expect a negative association between DForeign
and changes in cash ETRs. <sup>14</sup>

We include DLeverage to control for the changes in a firm’s capital structure. DLeverage equals the change in the ratio of
long-term debt to assets. Prior literature argues that debt provides an important tax shield (Graham 1996) and finds a negative
relation between leverage and marginal tax rates. Because interest deductions decrease income for both tax and financial
reporting purposes, it is unclear whether leverage would necessarily decrease effective tax rates. However, Newberry and
Dhaliwal (2001) argue that multinationals can place debt in high-tax locations to reduce their effective tax rates. Firms can also
structure off-balance sheet financing to maximize interest deductions without decreasing book income (Mills and Newberry
2004) or can structure debt to use foreign tax credits (Newberry 1998). Collectively, these studies suggest that increased levels
of debt are negatively associated with changes in effective tax rates.

We include DPP&E to proxy for tax planning opportunities that arise from capital assets. DPP&E equals the change in
ratio of property, plant, and equipment to total assets. Governments often use tax policy to spur economic investment,
especially during economic downturns. Consistent with legislated tax shields, capital-intensive firms have lower tax burdens
(Gupta and Newberry 1997), higher book-tax differences (Mills and Newberry 2001; Wilson 2009; Lisowsky 2010), and
higher Internal Revenue Service (IRS) deficiencies (Rice 1992; Mills 1998). Furthermore, many tax shelters during the 1990s
involved long-lived capital assets (McGill and Outslay 2004). As a result, we expect a negative relation between DPP&E and
changes in cash ETRs.

We include DInventory to proxy for changes in a firm’s inventory intensity. Because higher inventory intensity does not
typically generate tax planning opportunities, we anticipate a positive association between DInventory and changes in cash
ETRs.

We include DR&D to control for changes in intellectual property. DR&D equals the change in the ratio of research and
development expense to revenues. Intellectual property, such as patents and brand intangibles, increases opportunities to
decrease taxes via income shifting. The R&D tax credit also reduces cash ETRs. As such, we expect DR&D to be negatively
related to changes in cash ETRs.

We include DDiscAccruals to control for changes in financial reporting practices. DDiscAccruals equals the change in
pretax performance matched discretionary accruals as estimated in Frank, Lynch, and Rego (2009). Frank et al. (2009) find that
firms that exhibit more aggressive financial reporting practices are more tax aggressive. As such, we expect a negative
association between DDiscAccruals and changes in cash ETRs.

We include the change in an indicator variable (DNOL) to control for changes in the presence of net operating loss
carryforwards. Consistent with S. Chen, X. Chen, Cheng, and Shevlin (2010), we expect that NOL firms have lower tax rates

14 Given that we cannot measure the location of the constraint for multinational firms (i.e., firm-wide, domestic only, or foreign only), some of our sample
firms classified as constrained may be constrained domestically at the U.S. parent, but unconstrained internationally. These firms are likely to repatriate
foreign cash holdings to alleviate the constraint, which, given the high U.S. statutory rate, will likely result in additional U.S. taxes due upon
repatriation of foreign earnings. Repatriation taxes will increase the firm’s cash effective tax rate and empirically reduce our ability to detect an
association between financial constraints and tax planning. In a contemporaneous study, Dyreng and Markle (2013) examine the location of profits for
multinational corporations facing financial constraints and find evidence consistent with the conjecture that multinationals facing financial constraints
shift less profit overseas. In supplemental tests, we repeat our analysis using only firms that do not report foreign earnings to ensure that any
confounding effect related to repatriations is not materially impacting our results. All inferences hold.

IV. EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS


Sample

Table 1 summarizes our sample selection process and provides the number of observations used in the various empirical
tests. To investigate the effect of financial constraints on firms’ tax planning activities, we begin with firms listed on Compustat
from 1987, the first year cash taxes paid becomes available in Compustat due to Statement of Financial Accounting Standards
(SFAS) 95 requiring this disclosure, to 2011. Consistent with prior tax planning studies, in our main analysis, we eliminate
financial firms and utility firms, firm-year observations with missing or negative pretax income, and firm-year observations
missing data required to compute the tax planning and control variables used in our analyses. <sup>15</sup> We also require data to compute
the firm-specific financial constraint measures and the macroeconomic financial constraint measure based on changes in
economy-wide lending practices.
